description: Team SAR Cosmos is building an interactive 3D dashboard for the Dancing with the SARs challenge. Nepal has 21 glacial lakes classed as critically dangerous, and only 2 have proper mitigation. We combine NISAR radar, which sees through monsoon clouds, with optical satellite history to track six of these lakes. The site shows published lake areas now and will add our own satellite results once the pipeline runs. Our risk tiers measure growth, not flood probability.
summary:
SAR Cosmos is an interactive web project I built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge “Dancing with the SARs.” The idea is simple: Himalayan glacial lakes need to be monitored, but during the monsoon, clouds can make normal optical satellite images difficult to use. SAR Cosmos explores how optical data from Landsat and radar data from NASA-ISRO NISAR can work together for this problem.

The project focuses on six glacial lakes in Nepal. It includes a 3D Himalaya, lake-area history, an observation calendar, radar scene visualizations, and an interactive assistant called Cosmo. I also built Python processing pipelines using Google Earth Engine and NISAR GCOV data, with image processing methods to identify the lake-water area.

The goal is not to predict a GLOF or replace existing warning systems. Instead, SAR Cosmos is a way to make satellite observations easier to explore and show how radar could help keep watching these lakes when clouds get in the way.
details:
SAR Cosmos is an interactive web project our team built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge challenge “Dancing with the SARs.” Our project focuses on six glacial lakes in Nepal and explores how satellite data can help us monitor changes in these lakes.

The main idea behind SAR Cosmos is to bring together optical data from Landsat and radar data from NASA-ISRO NISAR. Optical satellite images can become difficult to use when clouds cover the Himalayas, while SAR can observe the Earth’s surface through clouds. By looking at both types of data, we can get a better idea of what is happening around these lakes.

We built an interactive website that includes a 3D view of the Himalayas, lake-area history, an observation calendar, radar visualizations, and an interactive assistant called Cosmo. We also developed Python-based processing pipelines for Landsat and NISAR data. Our NISAR pipeline works with GCOV radar data and includes steps for processing the radar images, reducing speckle noise, identifying water areas, checking the results, and calculating lake-water area.

We also created a simple risk indicator based on recent changes in lake area. It is meant to help users notice changes, not to predict a GLOF or replace an official warning system.

We used Python, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Google Earth Engine, NASA and USGS satellite resources, NISAR/ASF resources, and web visualization tools. We also used AI tools during development for coding assistance, debugging, documentation, and parts of the interface.

What makes SAR Cosmos different is that we tried to make the satellite data easier to explore instead of presenting it only as numbers or technical images. While building it, we considered things like cloud cover, the limitations of radar data, data reliability, ease of use, and making sure that measured data and our own indicators were clearly separated.

Our goal is to make satellite observations easier for people to understand and show how optical and radar data could work together to monitor Himalayan glacial lakes, especially during times when clouds make optical observations difficult.
